body.hook: Naturalists from Darwin to modern park wardens have one habit in common: they write everything down. A field journal turns a walk outside into real scientific observation.

study.title: The Field Journal
study.question: How do scientists record what they see outdoors?
study.passage:
Field journal setup (written for this lesson):
Every entry starts with: date, time, location, weather (temperature, cloud cover, wind) and who you're with.
Use all three: words (describe colours, sounds, smells, textures), pictures (labelled sketches with arrows, a scale like "about 5 cm") and numbers (counts, temperature, measurements).
Observation vs inference: "Five holes in the dead tree, each about 3 cm wide" is an observation. "A woodpecker made these holes" is an inference. Write inferences with "I think... because..."
Question prompts: "I notice... I wonder... It reminds me of..."
Activity (30 minutes outside): 1. Sit-spot: sit silently for 10 minutes in one spot; record everything you sense. 2. Sketch one living thing and one non-living thing with labels and a scale. 3. Count something (birds, ants, dandelions in a square metre). 4. Write two inferences and two questions.
Respect: observe without disturbing plants or animals.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

discussion: What did you notice in the sit-spot that you would normally miss?

body.objective: Students will be able to identify living and non-living parts.
body.iCan: I can identify living and non-living parts.
successCriteria: I can identify biotic and abiotic parts of an ecosystem
I can describe how living and non-living parts interact
I can record ecosystem parts at a local site
body.hook: A pond, a field or even a crack in the schoolyard pavement is an ecosystem: living things interacting with water, soil, air and sunlight. Every part depends on the others.

vocabulary.definition: Living things interacting with each other and their non-living surroundings.
Living or once-living parts of an ecosystem, such as plants, animals and fungi.
Non-living parts, such as water, soil, sunlight, air and temperature.
The place where an organism lives and gets what it needs.
An organism such as a fungus or bacterium that breaks down dead matter.
A way two parts of an ecosystem affect each other.

study.title: Living and Non-living
study.question: How do living and non-living things work together in an ecosystem?
study.passage:
Site survey (written for this lesson):
1. Hoop survey: groups place a hoop or a 1 m square on the ground in three spots (sunny grass, shady area, near water or a drain).
2. Biotic list: plants (grasses, dandelions, moss), animals (ants, beetles, worms, birds), fungi (mushrooms, lichens on rocks), signs of animals (tracks, droppings, chewed leaves).
3. Abiotic measurements: air and soil temperature, light (sunny, partial, shade), soil moisture (dry, damp, wet), soil type (sand, clay, loam), slope.
4. Interactions: draw arrows linking parts: sunlight → grass (energy); worms → soil (mixing); fungi → dead leaves (decomposition); shade → moss (cool, moist).
5. Compare the three spots: how do abiotic conditions change what lives there?
Respect: return rocks and logs exactly where they were; observe small animals without harm.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Place survey squares in three spots
discussion: Which spot had the most living things?
How did shade and moisture change what lived there?
study.product: Create an ecosystem diagram for one survey spot with at least six biotic and abiotic parts and four labelled interactions.

body.objective: Students will be able to map a study site.
body.iCan: I can map a study site.
successCriteria: I can draw a site map with a title, legend, compass rose and scale
I can measure distances by pacing
I can show habitats and features on my map
body.hook: Before scientists study an area, they map it. A good site map shows where things are, helps you return to the same spot, and reveals patterns you might miss on the ground.

vocabulary.definition: A drawing of a study area seen from above.

study.title: Mapping Our Site
study.question: How do I make an accurate map of a study site?
study.passage:
Mapping steps (written for this lesson):
1. Pace length: walk 10 m on a measured line and count your steps (count every step, or every second step as one "pace"). Divide 10 by your count to get metres per step (e.g. 10 m ÷ 14 steps ≈ 0.7 m).
2. Choose the site: about 30 m × 30 m of the schoolyard or a nearby park.
3. Find north: use a compass or the sun (in the afternoon the sun is in the southwest).
4. Measure the edges by pacing; convert to metres.
5. Choose a scale that fits your paper: e.g. 1 cm = 2 m.
6. Draw from a bird's-eye view: buildings, paths, trees, garden beds, drains, slopes.
7. Legend: symbols for trees, shrubs, grass, water, pavement, survey squares from last lesson.
8. Add title, your name, date, compass rose and scale bar.
Accuracy check: compare maps between groups; where do they disagree and why?
